reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder of oestrogen overproduction caused by gain-of-function rearrangements at the CYP19A1 locus that drive aromatase overexpression
Affected males present with prepubertal or peripubertal gynaecomastia, the hallmark feature, sometimes with small testes and reduced fertility
Excess oestrogen accelerates skeletal maturation, causing an early growth spurt but premature epiphyseal fusion and consequent short adult stature
Affected females may show macromastia, precocious or accelerated development and menstrual irregularity
Biochemistry shows elevated oestrogens with a raised oestrogen-to-androgen ratio and often suppressed gonadotropins
The condition contrasts sharply with aromatase deficiency, in which oestrogen is absent and stature is tall
Aromatase inhibition is the rational pharmacological approach to reduce oestrogen excess and preserve adult height, alongside management of gynaecomastia
reference.pathophysiology: Aromatase excess syndrome results from heterozygous genomic rearrangements (duplications, deletions or inversions) around CYP19A1 that place the aromatase coding sequence under constitutively active promoters, leading to widespread overexpression of the enzyme. Excess conversion of androgens to oestrogens raises circulating oestrogen levels, producing gynaecomastia in males and accelerated growth in both sexes. Because oestrogen drives epiphyseal maturation, the early growth acceleration is followed by premature fusion of the growth plates and a shortened final height. The oestrogen excess also feeds back on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, contributing to hypogonadism and impaired fertility.
additionalDifferentials: Liver disease or hyperthyroidism causing gynaecomastia
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with Sertoli cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: Serum oestradiol and oestrone with concurrent androgens to establish a raised oestrogen-to-androgen ratio
Gonadotropin measurement to assess suppression of the pituitary-gonadal axis
Molecular and cytogenetic analysis of the CYP19A1 locus for gain-of-function rearrangements
Bone age radiograph to document accelerated skeletal maturation
Testicular ultrasound and tumour markers to exclude an oestrogen-secreting tumour
Adrenal and hepatic imaging or biochemistry when a secondary cause is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive gynaecomastia or a testicular mass suggesting an oestrogen-secreting tumour
Accelerated bone age threatening early epiphyseal closure and short stature
Signs of an underlying malignancy or systemic disease as an alternative oestrogen source
Marked psychosocial distress from prominent gynaecomastia
reference.prognosis: With aromatase inhibition to lower oestrogen, growth potential can be partly preserved and gynaecomastia stabilised, though established breast tissue may require surgical correction. Untreated disease results in short adult stature and persistent gynaecomastia.
pitfalls: Dismissing early gynaecomastia as physiological and missing a familial oestrogen-excess disorder
Failing to exclude an oestrogen-secreting tumour before attributing symptoms to the syndrome
Overlooking accelerating bone age until height potential is lost
Confusing the phenotype with aromatase deficiency, which presents oppositely
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
